1
昔者元胎無象，太素流形，對越在天，以爲元首，則記所謂冬居營窟，夏居橧巢，飲血茹毛，未有麻絲者也。 及燧人鑽火，庖犧出震，風宗下武，炎胤昌基，畫野無聞，其歸一揆。 黃帝則東海南江，登空躡岱，至於崑峰振轡，崆山訪道，[1]存諸汗竹，不可厚誣。 高陽任地依神，帝嚳順天行義。 東踰蟠木，西濟流沙，北至幽陵，南撫交阯，日月所經，舟車所至，莫匪王臣，不踰茲域。 帝堯時，禹平水土，以爲九州。 虞舜登庸，厥功彌劭，表提類而分區宇，判山河而考疆域，冀北創并部之名，燕齊起幽營之號，則書所謂肇十有二州，封十有二山者也。 夏功在于唐堯，殷因無所損益。 周武克商，自豐徂鎬。 至成王時，改作禹貢，徐梁入於青雍，冀野析於幽并。 職方掌天下之土，以周厥利； 保章辯九州之野，皆有分星。 東南曰揚州，正南曰荊州，河南曰豫州，正東曰青州，河東曰兗州，正西曰雍州，東北曰幽州，河內曰冀州，正北曰并州。 始皇初并天下，懲{乂心}戰國，削罷列侯，分天下爲三十六郡。 〈三川、河東、南陽、南郡、九江、鄣郡、會稽、潁川、碭郡、泗水、薛郡、東郡、琅邪、齊郡、上谷、漁陽、右北平、遼西、遼東、代郡、鉅鹿、邯鄲、上黨、太原、雲中、九原、雁門、上郡、隴西、北地、漢中、巴郡、蜀郡、黔中、長沙，凡三十五郡，與內史爲三十六郡也。〉 於是興師踰江，平取百越，又置閩中、南海、桂林、象郡，凡四十郡，郡一守焉。 其地則西臨洮而北沙漠，東縈西帶，皆臨大海。 漢祖龍興，革秦之弊，分內史爲三部，更置郡國二十有三， 〈桂陽、江夏、豫章、河內、魏郡、東海、楚國、平原、梁國、定襄、泰山、汝南、淮陽、千乘、東萊、燕國、清河、信都、常山、中山、渤海、廣漢、涿郡，合二十三也。 三內史者，河上、渭南、中地也。 地理志曰：高祖增二十六，武帝改河上、渭南、中地以爲京兆、馮翊、扶風，是爲三輔也。〉 文增厥九， 〈廣平、城陽、淄川、濟南、膠西、膠東、河間、廬江、衡山，武帝改衡山曰「六安」。〉 景加其四。 〈濟北、濟陰、山陽、北海也。 宣改濟北曰東平。〉 武帝開越攘胡，初置十七， 〈南海、蒼梧、鬱林、合浦、交阯、九真、日南、珠崖、儋耳九郡，平西南夷置牂柯、越巂、沈黎、汶山、犍爲、益州六郡，西置武都郡，又分立零陵郡，合十七郡。〉 拓土分疆，又增十四。 〈弘農、臨淮、西河、朔方、酒泉、陳留、安定、天水、玄菟、樂浪、廣陵、敦煌、武威、張掖。〉 昭帝少事，又增其一。 〈金城也。〉 至平帝元始二年，凡新置郡國七十有一，與秦四十，合一百一十有一。 改雍曰涼，改梁曰益，又置徐州，復夏舊號，南置交阯，北有朔方，凡爲十三部。 〈涼、益、荊、揚、青、豫、兗、徐、幽、并、冀十一州，交阯、朔方二刺史，合十三部。〉 光武投戈之歲，在彫秏之辰，郡國蕭條，并省者八。 〈城陽、淄川、高密、膠東、六安、真定、泗水、廣陽。〉 建武十一年，省州牧，復爲刺史，員十三人，各掌一州。 明帝置一， 〈永昌也。〉 章帝置二， 〈任城、吳郡。〉 和順改作，其名有九。 〈和置濟北、廣陽，順改淮陽爲陳，改楚爲彭城，濟東爲東平，臨淮爲下邳，千乘爲六安，信都爲安平，天水爲漢陽。〉 省朔方刺史，合之於司隸，凡十三部， 〈其與西漢不同者，司隸校尉部郡治河南，朔方隸於并部。〉 而郡國百有八焉。 〈省前漢八，分置五，改舊名七，因舊九十六，少前漢三也。〉 桓靈頗增於前，復置六郡。 〈桓，高陽、高涼、博陵； 靈，南安、鄱陽、廬陵。〉 魏武定霸，三方鼎立，生靈版蕩，關洛荒蕪，所置者十二， 〈新興、樂平、西平、新平、略陽、陰平、帶方、譙、樂陵、章武、南鄉、襄陽。〉 所省者七， 〈上郡、朔方、五原、雲中、定襄、漁陽、廬江。〉 而文帝置七， 〈朝歌、陽平、弋陽、魏興、新城、義陽、[2]安豐。〉 明及少帝增二， 〈明，上庸也； 少，平陽也。〉 得漢郡者五十四焉。 蜀先主於漢建安之間初置郡九， 〈巴東、巴西、梓潼、江陽、汶山、漢嘉、朱提、宕渠、涪陵。〉 後主增二， 〈雲南、興古。〉 得漢郡者十有一焉。 吳主大皇帝初置郡五， 〈臨賀、武昌、珠崖、新安、廬陵南部。〉 少帝、景帝各四， 〈少，臨川、臨海、衡陽、湘東。 景，天門、建安、建平、合浦北部。〉 歸命侯亦置十有二郡， 〈始安、始興、邵陵、安成、新昌、武平、九德、吳興、東陽、桂林、滎陽、宜都。〉 得漢郡者十有八焉。
In the earliest age, before form took shape from undifferentiated simplicity, people looked to Heaven as their sovereign. The old texts describe them wintering in sunken huts, summering in treetop nests, consuming raw flesh and blood, long before cloth ever existed. Later came Suiren’s discovery of fire, Fuxi’s rise from the east, the succession of wind and flame that laid a prosperous foundation, and though we hear nothing yet of surveying the wilderness into domains, all these ages still point to a single underlying pattern. The Yellow Emperor is said to have traveled from the eastern sea to the southern rivers, climbed Kongsang and Mount Tai, climbed the Kunlun heights to pause his chariot, and sought the Dao on Kongtong; the tradition is written on ancient slips and should not be dismissed out of hand. Zhuanxu grounded his rule in the land and in communion with the spirits; Emperor Ku aligned his government with Heaven and with moral duty. Their sway ran east beyond the eastern frontier tree, west across the desert sands, north to the dark wastes, and south to Jiaozhi; under sun and moon, wherever chariot or ship could go, every people owed allegiance to the throne, and none lay outside this compass. Under Emperor Yao, Yu brought floods and terrain under control and organized the realm into the Nine Provinces. Once Shun took power, his accomplishments deepened: he sorted kinds of terrain to partition the world, traced ranges and rivers to fix boundaries, coined the Bing administration north of Ji, and named the You and Ying regions out of Yan and Qi—exactly the twelve provinces and twelve sacred peaks spoken of in the classics. The Xia order rested on the foundations Yao had laid; the Shang inherited that layout and left it unchanged. When King Wu overthrew Shang, the Zhou court shifted its seat from Feng to Hao. Under King Cheng the Yugong scheme was redrawn: Xu and Liang were folded into Qing and Yong, while the old Ji plain was divided between the new You and Bing sectors. The regional bureau mapped the empire’s lands and catalogued what each tract could yield; The astronomers correlated the nine provinces with the sky, assigning each region its own constellation. Yangzhou lay to the southeast, Jingzhou to the south, Yuzhou south of the Yellow River, Qingzhou to the east, Yanzhou east of the river, Yongzhou to the west, Youzhou to the northeast, Jizhou in the inner basin, and Bingzhou to the north. On first unifying China, the First Emperor, determined not to repeat the Warring States fragmentation, stripped the feudal lords of power and carved the empire into thirty-six commanderies. The gloss lists thirty-five outer commanderies—from Sanshi and Hedong through the northern and southern marches to Shu and Changsha—which, added to the capital intendant’s domain, made the famous thirty-six Qin commanderies. He then sent troops south of the great river, subdued the Yue peoples, and added Minzhong, Nanhai, Guilin, and Xiang, bringing the total to forty commanderies, each headed by a single appointed governor. The realm stretched west to the Tao River and north into the sands, girdled by mountains east and west, and everywhere opened toward the ocean. The Han founder, sweeping away Qin’s faults, divided the inner intendant into three jurisdictions and added twenty-three new commanderies and principalities, The new jurisdictions were Guiyang, Jiangxia, Yuzhang, Henei, Weijun, Donghai, Chu, Pingyuan, Liang, Dingxiang, Taishan, Runan, Huaiyang, Qiansheng, Donglai, Yan, Qinghe, Xindu, Changshan, Zhongshan, Bohai, Guanghan, and Zhuo—twenty-three units altogether. The inner domain was split among the Heshang, Weinan, and Zhongdi intendancies. The Han geography notes that Gaozu created twenty-six new units and that Emperor Wu reorganized Heshang, Weinan, and Zhongdi into Jingzhao, Fengyi, and Fufeng—the region later called the Three Adjuncts.〉 Emperor Wen added nine more domains, They were Guangping, Chengyang, Zichuan, Jinan, Jiaoxi, Jiaodong, Hejian, Lujiang, and Hengshan—the last of which Emperor Wu renamed Lu’an. Emperor Jing added four more. They were Jibei, Jiyin, Shanyang, and Beihai. Emperor Xuan redesignated Jibei as Dongping.〉 Emperor Wu pushed into the south and drove back the steppe peoples, initially founding seventeen new commanderies, The note counts nine southern coastal commands, six created from the southwestern Yi campaign, the new Wudu outpost in the west, and a detached Lingling—seventeen additions in total. As borders widened, fourteen more commanderies were carved out. They included Hongnong, Linhuai, Xihe, Shuofang, Jiuquan, Chenliu, Anding, Tianshui, Xuantu, Lelang, Guangling, Dunhuang, Wuwei, and Zhangye. Emperor Zhao, undertaking little else, added one more commandery. That addition was Jincheng commandery. By Emperor Ping’s Yuanshi 2, seventy-one new units had been created; added to the forty inherited from Qin, the empire counted one hundred eleven commanderies and kingdoms. Yong became Liang, Liang became Yi, Xu was revived under its ancient name, Jiaozhi was organized in the south, Shuofang guarded the north, and the whole was grouped into thirteen inspectorates. The thirteen regional circuits comprised eleven provinces plus the two special inspectorates at Jiaozhi and Shuofang. When Guangwu laid down the sword amid a ruined realm, eight redundant commanderies were folded together or struck from the rolls. The eight were Chengyang, Zichuan, Gaomi, Jiaodong, Lu’an, Zhending, Sishui, and Guangyang. In Jianwu 11 the Eastern Han restored the old inspector system—thirteen officials, each supervising a single province. Emperor Ming added one commandery, That unit was Yongchang commandery. Emperor Zhang added two more, They were Rencheng and Wu. During the He and Shun reigns nine further name changes or redesignations were recorded. He’s additions were Jibei and Guangyang; Shun’s edicts renamed Huaiyang to Chen, Chu to Pengcheng, Jidong to Dongping, Linhuai to Xiapi, Qiansheng to Lu’an, Xindu to Anping, and Tianshui to Hanyang. Shuofang’s inspectorate was folded into the capital Sili circuit, leaving thirteen regional units, Unlike Western Han, the Sili colonel’s district was administered from Henan, while Shuofang answered to Bing. The realm now comprised one hundred eight commanderies and kingdoms. Compared with Western Han, eight jurisdictions disappeared, five were newly split, seven were renamed, ninety-six carried over unchanged—three fewer in total. The Huan and Ling emperors expanded the map again, reinstating six commanderies. Huan’s additions were Gaoyang, Gaoliang, and Boling; Ling created Nan’an, Poyang, and Luling.〉 While Cao Cao seized northern hegemony amid the tripartite standoff and a devastated Guanzhong and Luoyang plain, he created twelve new commanderies, They were Xinxing, Leping, Xiping, Xinping, Lüeyang, Yinping, Daifang, Qiao, Leling, Zhangwu, Nanxiang, and Xiangyang. Seven older jurisdictions were eliminated, They included Shang, Shuofang, Wuyuan, Yunzhong, Dingxiang, Yuyang, and Lujiang. Emperor Wen of Wei then added seven more, They were Zhaoge, Yangping, the eastern Yiyang commandery, Weixing, Xincheng, the southern Yiyang garrison,[2] and Anfeng. Emperor Ming and the deposed Young Emperor each created two commanderies, Ming added Shangyong; the Young Emperor added Pingyang.〉 Wei therefore controlled fifty-four former Han commanderies. Between the late Han Jian’an years, Liu Bei initially carved nine new commanderies out of Shu, They were Badong, Baxi, Zitong, Jiangyang, Wenshan, Hanjia, Zhuti, Dangqu, and Fuling. Liu Shan later added two more, They were Yunnan and Xinggu. Shu altogether held eleven former Han commanderies. Sun Quan initially founded five commanderies, They were Linhe, Wuchang, Zhuya, Xin’an, and southern Luling. Sun Liang and Sun Xiu each added four commanderies, Sun Liang created Linchuan, Linhai, Hengyang, and Xiangdong; Sun Xiu added Tianmen, Jian’an, Jianping, and northern Hepu.〉 Sun Hao likewise carved out twelve new commanderies, They were Shi’an, Shixing, Shaoling, Ancheng, Xinchang, Wuping, Jiude, Wuxing, Dongyang, Guilin, Xingyang, and Yidu. Wu ultimately governed eighteen former Han commanderies.
2
晉武帝太康元年，既平孫氏，凡增置郡國二十有三， 〈滎陽、上洛、頓丘、臨淮、東莞、襄城、汝陰、長廣、廣甯、昌黎、新野、隨郡、陰平、義陽、毗陵、宣城、南康、晉安、寧浦、始平、略陽、樂平、南平。〉 省司隸置司州，別立梁、秦、寧、平四州，仍吳之廣州，凡十九州， 〈司、冀、兗、豫、荊、徐、揚、青、幽、平、并、雍、涼、秦、梁、益、寧、交、廣州。〉 郡國一百七十三， 〈仍吳所置二十五，仍蜀新置十一，仍魏所置二十一，仍漢舊九十三，置二十三。〉 以爲冠帶之國，盡有殷周之土。 若乃敦龐於天地之始，昭晰於犧農之世，用長黎元，未爭疆埸。 而玉環楛矢，夷裘風駕，南翬表貺，東風入律，光乎上德，奚遠弗臻。 然則星象麗天，山河紀地，端掖裁其弘敞，崤函判其都邑，仰觀俯察，萬物攸歸。 是以洛沚咸陽，宛然秦漢，晉濱河西，同知堯禹，于茲新邑，宅是鎬京，五尺童子皆能口誦者，史官弗之書也。
After Sima Yan crushed the Sun regime in Taikang 1, he reorganized the south with twenty-three new commanderies and kingdoms, They included Xingyang, Shangluo, Dunqiu, Linhuai, Dongguan, Xiangcheng, Ruyin, Changguang, Guangning, Changli, Xinye, Sui, Yinping, Yiyang, Piling, Xuancheng, Nankang, Jin’an, Ningpu, Shiping, Lüeyang, Leping, and Nanping. The Jin court replaced the Han Sili circuit with a new Sizhou, added Liang, Qin, Ning, and Ping, kept Wu’s Guangzhou, and thus organized nineteen provinces, The nineteen provinces were Si, Ji, Yan, Yu, Jing, Xu, Yang, Qing, You, Ping, Bing, Yong, the Hexi Liang circuit, Qin, the Hanzhong Liang circuit, Yi, Ning, Jiao, and Guang. The empire now counted one hundred seventy-three commanderies and kingdoms, Twenty-five came from Wu’s map, eleven from Shu’s additions, twenty-one from Wei’s roster, ninety-three survived unchanged from Han, and twenty-three were Jin’s own new units. As a civilized empire at the heart of the world, Jin encompassed all the lands once ruled by Shang and Zhou. In the primordial vastness before history, when Fuxi and Shennong brought clarity to human life, rulers simply nurtured their people and knew nothing of fighting over frontiers. Jade tokens and tribute arrows, furs borne in from the steppes, southern envoys presenting their gifts, spring winds harmonizing with the pitch-pipes—all testified to a virtue so brilliant that no corner of the world lay beyond its reach. Constellations pattern the sky while rivers and mountains inscribe the earth; the twin palace flanks frame the capital’s grandeur, the Xiao and Han passes define its seat of power—gazing upward and downward, every creature finds its allotted home. Everyone knows how the Luo heartland and Xianyang echo Qin and Han, how the Jin domain along the western river recalls the age of Yao and Yu, and how this new capital claims the mantle of old Hao—truths so familiar that every child repeats them, which is why the official histories pass them over in silence.
3
昔庖犧氏生於成紀，而爲天子，都於陳。 神農氏都陳，而別營于曲阜。 黃帝生於壽丘，而都於涿鹿。 少昊始自窮桑，而遷都曲阜。 顓頊始自窮桑，而徙邑商丘。 高辛即號，建都于亳。 孫卿子曰：「不登高山，不知天之高； 不臨深谿，不知地之厚也。 」大哉坤象，萬物資生，載崑華而不墜，傾河海而寧泄。 考卜惟王，乘飛駐軫，睨𡹮山而鐫勒，覽曾城以爲玩。 時逢稽浸，道接陵夷，平王東遷，星離豆剖，當塗馭宇，瓜分鼎立。 世祖武皇帝接千祀之餘，當八堯之禪，先王桑梓，罄宇來歸，斯固可得而言者矣。 惠皇不虞，中州盡棄，永嘉南度，綸行建鄴，九分天下而有二焉。
Legend places the birth of Fuxi’s clan at Chengji; as sovereigns they ruled from Chen. The house of Shennong ruled from Chen yet maintained another center at Qufu. The Yellow Emperor was born on Mount Shouqiu and established his capital at Zhuolu. Shaohao rose from Qiongsang and later shifted his seat to Qufu. Zhuanxu likewise started from Qiongsang before relocating his capital to Shangqiu. Emperor Ku assumed the throne and founded his capital at Bo. Xun Qing said, “Without climbing a lofty peak, you cannot grasp how high the sky reaches; If you never stand above a deep gorge, you have no measure of how thick the earth runs. The narrative then turns to praise the earth’s power: every living thing draws sustenance from it, it can bear up Kunlun and Mount Hua without failing, and it can pour the great rivers and oceans toward the abyss without ever running dry. Sovereigns divined their mandate, raced in swift chariots, paused to carve boastful inscriptions on sacred peaks, and toured tiered capitals as though they were pleasure grounds. Calamity dragged on, royal virtue ebbed, King Ping abandoned the west, and the world flew apart; then the Caos seized the throne and the land broke into contending thirds, each claiming a share of the ancient cauldrons. Emperor Wu, the dynastic founder, picked up a mandate long in the making, accepted Wei’s abdication as Yao once yielded to Shun, and watched the old royal heartlands and every quarter of the realm come over to him—events that plainly deserve narration. When Emperor Hui fell victim to coup and war, the heartland was abandoned; with the Yongjia exodus the court crossed the Yangtze and the imperial train made Jianye its seat, so that Jin retained only two of the nine traditional divisions of the realm.
4
昔大禹觀於濁河而受綠字，寰瀛之內可得而言也。 天有七星，地有七表； 天有四維，地有四瀆。 八紘之外，名爲八極。 地不足東南，天不足西北。 八極之廣，東西二億三萬一千三百里，南北二億三萬一千三百里。 自地至天，半八極之數，自下亦如之。 昔黃帝令豎亥步自東極，至于西極，五億十萬九千八百八步。 史臣案，凡周天積百七萬九百一十三里，徑三十五萬六千九百七十里。 所謂南北爲經，東西爲緯。 天有十二次，日月之所躔； 地有十二辰，王侯之所國也。 或因生得姓，因功命土，祁、酉、燕、齊，在乎茲域。
When Yu the Great stood by the turbid Yellow River and received the river chart, he gained a model by which the whole world within the four seas could be described. Just as the sky is marked by seven principal stars, so the earth is marked by seven frontier belts; The sky is hung on four cosmic stays, and the land is gouged by four mighty watercourses that carry the flood away. Beyond the encircling girdle that ropes in the known world lie the eight outermost reaches. The ground gives way to the southeast, while the empyrean gapes widest toward the northwest. From the eastern pole to the western spans two hundred thirty-one thousand three hundred li—and the same measure runs from south to north. The vault above measured half the span of the Eight Poles, and the same depth echoed below. Once the Yellow Emperor bade Shu Hai stride from sunrise to sunset; the tally came to five hundred nine thousand eight hundred eight measured paces. Court mathematicians reckoned heaven's circuit at 1,070,913 li and its diameter at 356,970 li. This is what is meant by naming north-south the warp and east-west the weft. Twelve lunar lodges score the sky—the highway of sun and moon; twelve earthly divisions underpin the map where lords and princes plant their altars of soil and grain. Some clans took names from ancestral seats, others earned fiefs for deeds done—and the old domains of Qi, You, Yan, and Qi all fall inside these bounds.

昔黃帝旁行天下，方制萬里，得百里之國萬區，則《周易》所謂「首出庶物，萬國咸寧」者也。 昔在帝堯，協和萬邦，制八家爲鄰，三鄰爲朋，三朋爲里，五里爲邑，十邑爲都，十都爲師，州十有二師焉。 夏后氏東漸于海，西被于流沙，南浮于江，而朔南暨聲教，窮豎亥所步，莫不率俾，會群臣於塗山，執玉帛者萬國。 於是九州之內，作爲五服。 天子之國，內五百里甸服，百里賦納總，二百里納銍，三百里納秸服，四百里粟，五百里米。 甸服外五百里侯服，百里采，二百里任，三百里候。 侯服外五百里綏服，三百里揆文教，二百里奮武衛。 綏服外五百里要服，三百里夷，二百里蔡。 要服外五百里荒服，三百里蠻，二百里流。 訖于四海，弼成五服，五服至于五千里。 夏德中微，遇有窮之亂。 少康中興，不失舊物。 自孔甲之後，以至于桀，諸侯相兼，其能存者三千餘國，方於塗山，十損其七矣。 成湯敗桀於焦，遷鼎於亳，伊摯、仲虺之徒，大明憲典。 王者之制爵祿，公侯伯子男凡五等。 天子之田方千里，公侯田方百里，伯七十里，子男五十里。 不能五十里者，不達於天子，附於諸侯，曰附庸。 凡四海之內九州，州方千里。 州建百里之國三十，七十里之國六十，五十里之國百有二十，凡二百一十國。 名山大澤不以封，其餘以爲附庸間田。 八州，州二百一十國。 天子之縣內，百里之國九，七十里之國二十有一，五十里之國六十有三，凡九十三國。 名山大澤不以班，其餘以祿士，以爲間田。 凡九州，千七百七十三國。 天子之元士，諸侯之附庸，不與。 天子百里之內以供官，千里之內以爲御，千里之外設方伯。 五國以爲屬，屬有長； 十國以爲連，連有帥； 三十國以爲卒，卒有正； 二百一十國以爲州，州有伯。 八州，八伯，五十六正，百六十八帥，三百三十六長。 八伯各以其屬屬於天子之老二人，分天下爲左右，曰二伯。 千里之內曰甸，千里之外曰采，曰流。 天子使其大夫爲三監，監於方伯之國，國三人。 天子之縣，內，諸侯祿也； 外，諸侯嗣也。 武王歸豐，監於二代，設爵惟五，分土惟三。 封同姓五十餘國，周公、康叔建於魯衛，各數百里。 太公封於齊，表東海者也。 凡一千八百國，布列於五千里內。 而太昊、黃帝之後，唐虞侯伯猶存。 大司徒以諸公之地封疆方五百里，其食者半； 諸侯之地方四百里，其食者參之一； 諸伯之地方三百里，其食者參之一； 諸子之地方二百里，其食者四之一； 諸男之地方百里，其食者四之一。 不易之地家百畝，一易之地家二百畝，再易之地家三百畝。 五家爲比，使之相保； 五比爲閭，使之相受； 四閭爲族，使之相葬； 五族爲黨，使之相救； 五黨爲州，使之相賙； 五州爲鄉，使之相賓。 小司徒以五人爲伍，五伍爲兩，四兩爲卒，五卒爲旅，五旅爲師，五師爲軍。 以起軍旅，以作田役，以比追胥，以令貢賦。 乃經土地而井牧其田野，九夫爲井，四井爲邑，四邑爲丘，四丘爲甸，四甸爲縣，四縣爲都。 遺人則十里有廬，廬有飲食。 三十里有宿，宿有路室，路室有委。 五十里有市，市有候，候有館，館有積。 遂人則五家爲鄰，五鄰爲里，四里爲酇，五酇爲鄙，五鄙爲縣，五縣爲遂。 大司馬以九畿之籍，施邦國之政。 方千里曰國畿，其外方五百里曰侯畿，又其外方五百里曰甸畿，又其外方五百里曰男畿，又其外方五百里曰采畿，又其外方五百里曰衛畿，又其外方五百里曰蠻畿，又其外方五百里曰夷畿，又其外方五百里曰鎮畿，又其外方五百里曰藩畿。 〈畿，田限也。 自王城以外，面五千里爲界，有分限者九也。〉 于時治致太平，政稱刑措，民口千三百七十一萬四千九百三十三，蓋周之盛者也。 其衰也，則禮樂征伐出自諸侯，強吞弱而眾暴寡。 春秋之初，尚有千二百國，迄獲麟之末，二百四十二年，弒君三十六，亡國五十二，諸侯奔走不得保其社稷者不可勝數，而見於春秋經傳者百有七十國焉。 百三十九知其所居， 〈魯、邾、鄭、宋、紀、衛、西虢、莒、齊、陳、杞、蔡、邢、郕、晉、薛、許、鄧、秦、曹、楚、隨、黃、梁、虞、鄖、小邾、徐、燕、鄀、麋、舒、庸、郯、萊、吳、越、有窮、三苗、瓜州、有虞、東虢、共、宿、申、夷、向、南燕、滕、凡、戴、息、郜、芮、魏、淳于、穀、巴、州、蓼、羅、賴、牟、葛、譚、蕭、遂、滑、權、鄣、霍、耿、江、冀、弦、道、柏、微、鄫、厲、項、密、任、須句、顓臾、頓、管、雍、畢、豐、邘、應、蔣、茅、胙、夔、介、焦、沈、六、巢、根牟、唐、黎、郇瑕、寒、有鬲、斟灌、斟尋、過、有過、戈、偪陽、邿、鑄、豕韋、唐杜、楊、豳、鄶、觀、扈、邳、胡、黎、大庭、駘、岐、邶、鍾吾、蒲姑、昆吾、房、密須、甲父、鄅、桐、亳、韓、趙。〉 三十一國盡亡其處， 〈祭、極、荀、賈、貳、軫、絞、於餘丘、陽、箕、英氏、毛、聃、莘、偪、封父、仍、有仍、崇、鄟、庸、姺、奄、商奄、褒姒、蓐、有緡、闕鞏、飂、鬷、窮桑。〉 蠻夷戎狄不在其間。 五伯迭興，總其盟會。 陵夷至于戰國，遂有七王， 〈韓、魏、趙、燕、齊、秦、楚。〉 又有宋、衛、中山，不斷如綫，如三晉篡奪，亦稱孤也。
Long ago the Yellow Emperor quartered the realm, squared a domain ten thousand li on a side, and carved it into ten thousand hundred-li polities—the very epoch the Book of Changes extols when it says, "He who rises first above the throng brings every kingdom to rest." Under Yao the countries learned concord, and government knit tight: eight families made a street, three streets a cluster, three clusters a ward, five wards a market town, ten such towns a greater burgh, ten burghs a canton, and twelve cantons stitched one province. The Xia stretched east until the tide foamed at their feet, west to the shifting sands, south along the great rivers, until their transforming influence ran from pole to pole as far as Shu Hai had ever measured; none refused homage. At Mount Tu they gathered the lords, and ten thousand courts arrived with jade disks and silk. Within the Nine Provinces they layered five concentric belts of fealty. Around the capital ran five hundred li of royal fields: the inner ring sent whole stalks bundled, the next matured heads, the third straw and labor, the fourth threshed grain, the outermost polished rice for the palace kettle. Beyond that stretched another five hundred li of baronial land: the first hundred fed royal manors, the next two hundred supplied ministers of trust, the outer three hundred patrolled the marches. Next came five hundred li meant to "soothe": three hundred for schools and rites, two hundred bristling with spears that guarded the cordon. Outside the pacified belt lay five hundred li of "treaty" ground—three hundred li of loosely ruled bordermen, two hundred more under banishment law. The rim was five hundred li of wilderness—three hundred left to rough hill tribes, two hundred reserved for the river of banishment. The pattern ran to the four seas, the five girdles locked in place, a full five thousand li from throne to tide-line. Halfway through their age the Xia lost heart, and the realm reeled beneath Youqiong's revolt. Shaokang rallied the line and never surrendered the ancestral cauldrons. From Kong Jia to tyrant Jie the lords devoured one another until barely three thousand states remained—seven in ten had vanished since the great conference at Mount Tu. Cheng Tang broke Jie at Jiao and carried the tripods to Bo; ministers like Yi Yin and Zhong Hui lit clear lamps of law and precedent. Royal custom fixed five noble ranks—from duke down to baron—each with its stipend. The king measured a thousand li square; dukes and marquises a hundred, earls seventy, viscounts and barons a bare fifty on a side. Polities shy of fifty li could not seek audience alone; they hung on greater lords as client domains. Within the four seas lay nine provinces, each a thousand-li square on the chart. Each province raised thirty great hundred-li realms, sixty middling seventy-li counties, and a hundred twenty small fifty-li cells—two hundred ten banners in all. Crown peaks and imperial bogs never left the king's ledger; leftover patches became vassal pockets and buffer strips. Eight of the nine provinces repeated that pattern—two hundred ten states apiece. Inside the royal demesne itself stood nine hundred-li seats, twenty-one seventy-li manors, and sixty-three fifty-li plots—ninety-three realms devoted to the throne. Sacred heights and royal marshes were never fiefed away; the scraps paid stipendiary officials and plugged holes between grants. Across the Nine Provinces the tallies listed one thousand seven hundred seventy-three states. The count omits the king's senior householders and the petty clients of great barons. The inner hundred li fed the bureaucracy, the thousand li stocked palace service, and beyond that the king set regional elders to rule in his stead. Five states formed a dependency cluster led by a chief. Ten states formed a league placed under a captain. Thirty states formed a corps overseen by a senior marshal. Two hundred ten states formed a province ruled by a regional elder. Eight provinces meant eight great lords, fifty-six marshals, one hundred sixty-eight captains, and three hundred thirty-six village heads. Each provincial lord knelt to one of the king's two senior regents, splitting the world into eastern and western halves—the Two Chiefs of high Zhou. Inside the thousand-li cordon lay the royal hearths; outside stretched ministerial estates and the flowing lands of exile. The king posted three-man inspectorates in every regional capital to eye the barons for him. Domains hugging the throne were stipendiary grants to great lords. Those farther out settled into noble lines handed down through inheritance. King Wu withdrew to Feng, studied Xia and Shang, fixed five noble rows, and sorted fief size into three steps. He planted more than fifty Zhou princes across the map—the Duke of Zhou at Lu, Kang Shu at Wei—each commanding several hundred li. Tai Gong took Qi as his shield against the eastern tide. Eighteen hundred realms checkered the five-thousand-li heartland. Lines sprung from Taihao and the Yellow Emperor, marquises who remembered Yao and Shun, still clung to titles in that new Zhou dawn. The Minister of Education carved dukes five hundred li square but let them tax only half the soil; marquises held four hundred li yet drew a third to their kitchens; earls kept three hundred li with the same third rule; viscounts two hundred li but spent only a quarter; barons a bare hundred li yet owned a quarter of the yield. Permanent fields granted a household a hundred mu, once-fallow soil two hundred, and thrice-tired ground three hundred so the tax base stayed even. Five families swore mutual bail; five such rings a lane that housed the homeless; four lanes a clan burying its dead together; five clans a company that rushed to fires and raids; five companies a canton pooling famine grain; five cantons a countryside whose elders still bowed in guest-rite. The junior steward stacked squads: five men a file, five files a pair, four pairs a company, five companies a battalion, five battalions a host, five hosts the full army. Those ladders raised campaigns, drafted ditch gangs, mustered night watchmen, and split the grain and corvée rolls. Surveyors laid the well-net: nine farmers to a well, four wells a hamlet, four hamlets a hill-girdle, four hill-girdles a parcel, four parcels a county, four counties a great city. Wayfarers found a lodge every ten li with water and a warm bowl. Every thirty li brought a full station, roadside cells, and stacked grain. Every fifty li markets bustled with guard posts, guest halls, and piled stores. Rural marshals wove five homes into a lane, five lanes a hamlet, four hamlets a township, five townships a patch, five patches a county, five counties a sui belt. The war minister read the nine belts girding Wangcheng and from them spun every lord's marching orders. The capital sat in a thousand-li square; then nine half-thousand-li rings unrolled—baronial fields, royal estates, male fiefs, salary lands, guard strips, southern wilds, eastern wilds, garrison marches, and a final curtain of outer vassals. The marginal note explains that ji denotes the border of taxable fields. It adds that from the royal walls each quarter runs five thousand li, ringed by nine stepped partitions. That age ripened into the Great Peace, the racks stood empty, and the census inked 13,714,933 names—a Zhou summer at flood tide. When it rotted, drums and odes marched under barons' banners, strong states swallowed weak neighbors, and packs harried the lone. Early Spring and Autumn still counted twelve hundred flags; by the day Confucius penned the unicorn's close—two hundred forty-two bloodied years—thirty-six kings had been knifed, fifty-two realms snuffed, and numberless lords fled ruined shrines, though the classic and its gloss remember only one hundred seventy names. One hundred thirty-nine of them still have identifiable capitals on the map. The gloss strings together more than a hundred collateral polities—from Lu, Zhu, Zheng, Song, Ji, Wei, Western Guo, Ju, Qi, Chen, Qi (of the east), Cai, Xing, Cheng, Jin, Xue, Xu, Deng, Qin, Cao, Chu, Sui, Huang, Liang, Yu, Yun, Lesser Zhu, Xu, Yan, Ruo, Mi, Shu, Yong, Tan, Lai, Wu, and Yue through Youqiong, Sanmiao, Guazhou, You Yu, Eastern Guo, Gong, Su, Shen, Yi, Xiang, Southern Yan, Teng, Fan, Dai, Xi, Gao, Rui, Wei, Chunyu, Gu, Ba, Zhou, Liao, Luo, Lai, Mou, Ge, Tan, Xiao, Sui, Hua, Quan, Zhang, Huo, Geng, Jiang, Ji, Xian, Dao, Bo, Wei, Zeng, Li, Xiang, Mi, Ren, Xuqu, Zhuanyu, Dun, Guan, Yong, Bi, Feng, Yu, Ying, Jiang, Mao, Zuo, Kui, Jie, Jiao, Shen, Liu, Chao, Genmou, Tang, Li, Xunxia, Han, Youge, Zhuguan, Zhunxun, Guo, Youguo, Ge, Biyang, Shi, Zhu, Shangwei, Tang Du, Yang, Bin, Kuai, Guan, Hu, Li, Danting, Tai, Qi, Bei, Zhongwu, Pugu, Kunwu, Fang, Mixu, Jiafu, Yu, Tong, Bo, Han, and Zhao—whose lost seats later scholars can still roughly place from the classics and commentaries. Thirty-one others vanished so completely that their very sites are forgotten. The note preserves a further stratum of half-legendary seats—Zhai, Ji, Xun, Jia, Er, Zhen, Jiao, Yuyuqiu, Yang, Ji, Ying, Mao, Dan, Shen, Bi, Fengfu, Reng, Youreng, Chong, Tuan, Yong, Shen, Yan, Shangyan, Baosi, Ru, Youmin, Quegong, Liu, Zong, and Qiongsang—names that survive now chiefly as pale traces in exegetical literature. Southern, eastern, western, and northern tribes were never part of that roll. Five overlords rose in turn to chair the league altars and stamp clan oaths. The slide ran on into the Warring States, and seven crowned powers shouldered the world— Han, Wei, Zhao, Yan, Qi, Qin, and Chu. Song, Wei, and Zhongshan still hung by a thread, while the breakaway triplets of Jin stole the mandate yet whimpered that they ruled as orphaned heirs.

《司馬法》廣陳三代，曰：古者六尺爲步，步百爲畝，畝百爲夫，夫三爲屋，屋三爲井。 井方一里，是爲九夫，八家共之。 一夫一婦受私田百畝，公田十畝，是爲八百八十畝，餘二十畝爲廬舍，出入相友，守望相助，疾病相救。 民受田，上田夫百畝，中田夫二百畝，下田夫三百畝，歲受耕之，爰自其處。 其家眾男爲餘夫，亦以口受田如此。 士工商家受田，五口乃當農夫一口。 有賦有稅，稅謂公田什一及工商衡虞之入也，賦供車馬甲兵士從之役。 民年二十受田，六十歸田。 種穀必雜五種，以備災旱。 田中不得有樹，以妨五穀。 環廬種桑柘，菜茹有畦，瓜瓠果蓏植於疆埸，雞㹠狗豕無失其時。 閭有序，鄉有庠，序以明教，庠以行禮。 司馬之法，官設六軍之眾，因井田而制軍。 令地方一里爲井，井十爲通，通十爲成，成方十里。 成十爲終，終十爲同，同方百里。 同十爲封，封十爲畿，畿方千里。 故井四爲邑，邑四爲丘，丘十六井，有戎馬一匹，牛三頭。 四丘爲甸，甸六十四井也，有戎馬四匹，兵車一乘，牛十二頭，甲士三人，卒七十二人。 是謂乘車之制。 一同百里，提封萬井，除山川、坑岸、城池、邑居、園囿、街路三千六百井，定出賦六千四百井，戎馬四百匹，兵車百乘，此卿大夫菜地之大者也，是謂百乘之家。 一封三百六十六里，提封十萬井，定出賦六萬四千井，戎馬四千匹，兵車千乘，此謂諸侯之大者也，謂之千乘之國。 天子畿內方千里，提封百萬井，定出賦六十四萬井，戎馬四萬匹，兵車萬乘，戎卒七十二萬人，故天子稱萬乘之主焉。
The Military Canons of Sima recount the Three Ages: six feet to the pace, a hundred paces to the survey mu, a hundred mu to a husband's share, three husbands to a cluster, three clusters to the sacred well of nine farms. Each well squared a li, carved nine strips, and yoked eight families to its central lord's strip. Each couple drew a hundred private mu and ten for the common furrow—880 mu under tillage and twenty for roofs; neighbors pledged friendship at every gate, stood night watch together, and nursed fevers shoulder to shoulder. Farmers drew graded plots—one hundred mu on rich soil, two hundred on middling, three hundred on lean—rotating with the seasons as the law nudged them along. Extra grown sons counted as surplus tillers and earned more acreage by the same mouth tally. Gentry, craftsmen, and merchants held land too, yet five of their mouths paid as one plowman's share. Two ledgers ran: "tax" skimmed the lord's tenth and the townsmen who trafficked scales and marshes; "levy" horseshoed chariots, buckled armor, and dragooned footmen. A man took land at twenty and surrendered it at sixty. Every field blended five grains so famine could not kill the harvest whole. Grain land stayed shadeless—no orchard stealing sunlight from the staples. Mulberries hugged each roof, kitchen gardens squared their rows, melons straggled along the headlands, and every yard timed its fowl and hogs to the turning moons. Each lane kept a school where royal lessons shone, each district a hall where elders rehearsed ceremony. The war statutes called up six hosts, threading regiment on regiment straight from the well-field grid. Under the statute, one square li formed a jing, ten jing made a tong, ten tong a cheng, and a cheng stood ten li to the side. A stack of ten cheng became a zhong; ten zhong a tong, and each tong measured a hundred li on a side. Ten tong made a feng; ten feng a royal ringland (ji), a thousand li on every side—the core demesne of the crown. So four jing grouped into a yi, four yi into a qiu holding sixteen jing, supporting one mount for war and three draft oxen. Four qiu formed a dian of sixty-four jing, fit for four chargers, a single battle chariot, twelve oxen, three armored men, and seventy-two rank-and-file troops. This defined the military levy for one chariot. For a single tong, a hundred li on a side and ten thousand jing under seal, once mountains, waters, wasteland, fortifications, settlements, hunting parks, and roads had been set aside—three thousand six hundred jing—the remaining sixty-four hundred jing furnished four hundred mounts and a full hundred chariots; that was the largest estate granted to ministers and great officers, the so-called household of a hundred chariots. A feng of three hundred sixty-six li to the side embraced a hundred thousand jing, with sixty-four thousand taxable jing sustaining four thousand horses and a thousand chariots—the scale of the greatest feudal lords, a true thousand-chariot polity. Across the royal thousand-li square, a million jing yielded taxable ground for sixty-four myriad jing, mounting forty thousand horses, ten thousand chariots, and seven hundred twenty thousand soldiers—whence the sovereign earned the title of ruler of ten thousand chariots.

秦始皇既得志於天下，訪周之敗，以爲處士橫議，諸侯尋戈，四夷交侵，以弱見奪，於是削去五等焉。 漢興，創艾亡秦孤立而敗，於是割裂封疆，立爵二等，功臣侯者百有餘邑。 于時民罹秦項，戶口彫弊，大侯不過萬家，小者五六百戶，而尊王子弟，大啟九國。 古者有分土而無分民，若乃大者跨州連郡，小則十有餘城，以戶口爲差降，略封疆之遠近，所謂分民自漢始也。 起雁門以東，盡遼陽，爲燕代。 常山以南，太行左轉，渡河濟，漸于海，爲齊趙。 穀泗以注，奄有龜蒙，爲梁楚。 東帶江湖，薄會稽，爲荊吳。 北界淮瀕，略廬衡，爲淮南。 波漢之陽，亙九疑，爲長沙。 諸侯比境，周匝三垂，外接胡越。 天子自有三河、東郡、潁川、南陽，自江陵以西至巴蜀，北至雲中，西至隴西，與京師內史，凡十五郡。 文帝采賈生之議分齊趙，景帝用朝錯之計削吳楚。 武帝施主父之冊，下推恩之令，使諸侯王得分戶邑以封子弟，不行黜陟，而藩國自析。 自此以來，齊分爲七，趙分爲六，梁分爲五，淮南分爲三。 皇子始立者大國不過十餘城，長沙、燕、代雖有舊名，皆亡南北邊矣。 自文景與民休息，至平帝元始二年，民戶千二百二十三萬三千六十二，口五千九百五十九萬四千九百七十八，其地東西九千三百二里，南北萬三千三百六十八里。 大率十里一亭，亭有長。 十亭一鄉，鄉有三老，有秩嗇夫、游徼各一人。 縣大率方百里，民稠則減，稀則曠，鄉亭亦如之。 皆秦制也。 光武中興，不踰前制，東海王彊以去就有禮，故優以大封，兼食魯郡二十九縣，其餘稱爲寵錫者，兼一郡而已。 至桓帝永壽三年，戶千六十七萬七千九百六十，口五千六百四十八萬六千八百五十六，[3]斯亦戶口之滋殖者也。 獻帝建安元年拜曹操爲鎮東將軍，封費亭侯。 魏文帝黃初三年，初制封王之庶子爲鄉公，嗣王之庶子爲亭侯，[4]公侯之庶子爲亭伯。 劉備章武元年，亦以郡國封建諸王，或遙採嘉名，不由檢土地所出。 其戶二十萬，男女口九十萬。 孫權赤烏五年，亦取中州嘉號封建諸王。 其戶五十二萬三千，男女口二百四十萬。 晉文帝爲晉王，命裴秀等建立五等之制，惟安平郡公孚邑萬戶，制度如魏諸王。 其餘縣公邑千八百戶，地方七十五里； 大國侯邑千六百戶，地方七十里； 次國侯邑千四百戶，地方六十五里； 大國伯邑千二百戶，地方六十里； 次國伯邑千戶，地方五十五里； 大國子邑八百戶，地方五十里； 次國子邑六百戶，地方四十五里； 男邑四百戶，地方四十里。 [5]武帝泰始元年，封諸王以郡爲國。 邑二萬戶爲大國，置上中下三軍，兵五千人； 邑萬戶爲次國，置上軍下軍，兵三千人； 五千戶爲小國，置一軍，兵千五百人。 王不之國，官於京師。 罷五等之制，公侯邑萬戶以上爲大國，五千戶以上爲次國，不滿五千戶爲小國。 太康元年，平吳，大凡戶二百四十五萬九千八百四十，口一千六百一十六萬三千八百六十三。 而江左諸國並三分食一，元帝渡江，太興元年，始制九分食一。
Once Qin Shihuang had mastered the realm, he read Zhou's fall as the fruit of unbridled private debate among scholars, incessant war among lords, and relentless barbarian pressure that preyed on weakness—and scrapped the entire five-rank aristocracy. Han, still smarting from Qin's rigid centralization and swift ruin, reapportioned the map into fiefs, limited noble rank to two tiers, and let more than a hundred merit marquises each hold a patch of soil. Households were still shattered by Qin exactions and Chu civil war, so even great marquisates counted fewer than ten thousand families and small ones only five or six hundred—yet the throne lavished titles on imperial kinsmen and planted nine sprawling royal domains. Ancient kings had parceled soil, not registered subjects; now the largest apanages covered whole provinces, the modest still held a dozen walled towns, and rank tracked headcounts while the distances of frontiers hardly mattered—the peculiar Han practice of parting the people among lords had begun. The block running east from the Yanmen line through Liaoyang was reckoned as Yan and Dai together. South of Changshan, with the Taihang swinging east, the Yellow River and Ji ford behind them, and the coast ahead, stretched Qi and Zhao as one bloc. Between the Gu and Si confluence and the Gui-Meng massif lay the territories reckoned as Liang and Chu. A strip belted by the great river and southern lakes, nosing to Kuaiji, counted as Jing and Wu. North along the Huai's bank, drawing in the Lu and Heng ranges, stood the block called Huainan. North of the Han sweep and through the Jiuyi peaks ran the Changsha alignment. The vassals stood shoulder to shoulder along the inner rim, girdling three frontiers while opening outward onto the Hu steppe and southern Yue. Fifteen commanderies—the Three He core plus Dong, Yingchuan, and Nanyang, the western arc from Jiangling through Ba and Shu, the northern bastions Yunzhong, the Longxi line, and the metropolitan Neishi—remained directly in the emperor's hand. Han Wendi split Qi and Zhao on Jia Yi's advice; Jingdi pared the great eastern kingdoms with Chao Cuo's stratagem. Wudi promulgated Zhufu Yi's memorial as the "push-the-grace" edict, letting every king slice his domain to enfeoff heirs—no formal downgrading needed—and watched the great apanages quietly fracture. Thereafter Qi splintered seven ways, Zhao six, Liang five, Huainan three. A freshly minted imperial son might rule barely a dozen counties; mighty old names like Changsha, Yan, and Dai had become hollow titles stripped of their former north and south marches. The restorative reigns of Wen and Jing carried down to Pingdi's Yuanshi 2 (1 CE), when the registers recorded 12,233,062 households and 59,594,978 people across 9,302 li east–west and 13,368 li north–south. Roughly every ten li stood a courier lodge (ting) headed by a chief. Ten ting formed a township with three elders plus a single salaried sefu and a roving constable. A county normally covered a hundred-li square, trimmed where crowded, widened where thin, township and lodge scales following suit. Every one of these rules descended from Qin. When Guangwu revived Han he held to the old ceilings—except Liu Qiang, Prince of Donghai, whose scrupulous conduct in yielding the crown earned him a double stipend through twenty-nine Lu counties while other favorites merely tacked on a single commandery. By Huan's Yongshou 3 (157 CE) the rolls listed 10,677,960 households and 56,486,856 souls—clear evidence that the people were breeding back. In Xian's first year of Jian'an, Cao Cao received appointment as General Who Stabilizes the East and an enfeoffment as Marquis of the Feiting precinct. Huangchu 3 assigned a king's younger sons by secondary consorts the rank of village duke, an heir-apparent's younger brothers by secondary consorts the rank of precinct marquis, and a duke's or marquis's younger sons by secondary consorts the rank of precinct baron. Zhangwu 1 watched Liu Bei enfeoff his kinsmen with commandery-sized kingdoms, sometimes borrowing glamorous Central Plain toponyms that bore little relation to local revenue. That realm counted two hundred thousand households and nine hundred thousand persons all told. In his fifth Chiwu year Sun Quan did the same, granting his kinsmen splendid Central-Plain sobriquets. His domains mustered 523,000 households and 2,400,000 people. As Jin's king-maker Sima Zhao ordered Pei Xiu to draft the five noble ranks: only Sima Fu, duke of Anping commandery, kept the full ten-thousand-household scale befitting a Wei royal. Other county-level dukes held 1,800 households across seventy-five li to the side. Senior-grade marquises drew 1,600 households over seventy li. Next-rank marquises held 1,400 households across sixty-five li. Senior earls received 1,200 households within sixty li. Junior earls kept a thousand households spread over fifty-five li. Senior viscounts had eight hundred households inside fifty li. Lesser viscounts owned six hundred households across forty-five li. Lowest baronies stopped at four hundred households and forty li. Taishi 1 made each prince's kingdom co-extensive with an entire commandery. A great kingdom—20,000 registered households—fielded upper, middle, and lower brigades totaling 5,000 men. Secondary realms of ten thousand households maintained upper and lower corps with 3,000 troops. Petty kingdoms of 5,000 families mustered a single army of 1,500. Princes stayed in Luoyang on court salary rather than residing in their nominal realms. After the five-rank scheme lapsed, ducal or marquisal estates of ten thousand households or more counted as great polities, those from five thousand upward as secondary, and those below five thousand as small. Taikang 1, the year Wu fell, the empire tallied roughly 2,459,840 households and 16,163,863 mouths. South of the river every apanage skimmed a third of its host commandery until Yuan crossed; Taixing 1 trimmed the royal share to one-ninth.

案禹貢豫州之地。 及漢武帝，初置司隸校尉，所部三輔、三河諸郡。 其界西得雍州之京兆、馮翊、扶風三郡，北得冀州之河東、河內二郡，東得豫州之弘農、河南二郡，郡凡七。 位望隆于牧伯，[6]銀印青綬。 及光武都洛陽，司隸所部與前漢不異。 魏氏受禪，即都漢宮，司隸所部河南、河東、河內、弘農并冀州之平陽，合五郡，置司州。 晉仍居魏都，乃以三輔還屬雍州，分河南立滎陽，分雍州之京兆立上洛，廢東郡立頓丘，遂定名司州，以司隸校尉統之。 州統郡一十二，縣一百，戶四十七萬五千七百。 [7]
The chapter tracks the Yu Province demarcated in the "Tribute of Yu." Han Wudi created the Colonel Director of Retainers to oversee the three metropolitan adjuncts and the Three Rivers commanderies. The colonel's seven commanderies drew Jingzhao, Fengyi, and Fufeng from Yongzhou, Hedong and Henei from Jizhou, and Hongnong and Henan from Yuzhou. The colonel outranked provincial shepherds, badge by silver seal and green ribbon. Guangwu's move to Luoyang left the colonel's remit matching Western Han's footprint. Cao Wei inherited Luoyang's palaces, folded Henan, Hedong, Henei, Hongnong, and Pingyang commandery from Jizhou into a five-commandery Sizhou. Western Jin stayed put but reassigned the three Qin adjuncts back to Yong, carved Xingyang out of Henan, Shangluo out of Jingzhao, traded Dong commandery for Dunqiu, and locked the new layout under the colonel's eye. This Sizhou ruled twelve commanderies, one hundred counties, and 475,700 households. Here the edition inserts a marginal gloss in the commentary tradition.

永嘉之後，司州淪沒劉聰。 聰以洛陽爲荊州，及石勒，復以爲司州。 石季龍又分司州之河南、河東、弘農、滎陽，兗州之陳留、東燕爲洛州。 元帝渡江，亦僑置司州於徐，非本所也。 後以弘農人流寓尋陽者僑立爲弘農郡。 又以河東人南寓者，於漢武陵郡孱陵縣界上明地僑立河東郡，統安邑、聞喜、永安、臨汾、弘農、譙、松滋、大戚八縣。 [12]並寄居焉。 永和五年，桓溫入洛，復置河南郡，屬司州。
When Yongjia shattered the north, Sizhou passed into Liu Cong's hands. Liu Cong redesignated Luoyang as Jingzhou, but once Shi Le held the city the old name Sizhou returned. Shi Hu, styled Jilong, then prised Henan, Hedong, Hongnong, and Xingyang from Sizhou, joined them to Chenliu and Dongyan taken from Yanzhou, and called the new circuit Luozhou. After Sima Rui forded the great river as Prince of Langya and later Yuan Emperor of Jin, a shadow Sizhou was planted at Xu, far from its homeland. Refugees from Hongnang who washed up at Xunyang received a paper commandery that bore their old name. Hedong refugees were granted a paper commandery at Shangming, straddling the line of Chanling in the old Han circuit of Wuling, and the statute listed Anyi, Wenxi, Yong'an, Linfen, Hongnong, Qiao, Songzi, and Daqi—the full count of eight counties. Every clan was entered on the books as temporary residents. When Huan Wen marched into Luoyang in Yonghe 5, Henan commandery rose again on the statute book inside Sizhou.

案禹貢濟河之地，舜置十二牧，則其一也。 《周禮》：「河東曰兗州。 」《春秋元命包》云：「五星流爲兗州。 兗，端也，[13]信也。 」又云：「蓋取兗水以名焉。 」漢武帝置十三州，以舊名爲兗州，自此不改。 州統郡國八，縣五十六，戶八萬三千三百。
The "Tribute of Yu" describes the country between the Ji and the great river; there Shun once posted twelve regional shepherds, and this tract was among them. "East of the Yellow River," says the "Rites of Zhou," "men name that territory Yanzhou." The esoteric "Yuanchunbao" adds that the five wandering stars pour their light into Yanzhou. The gloss plays on the graph: "Yan" carries the sense of being straight, and of being trustworthy. The same text supposes people took the name from a Yan River threading the plain. When Emperor Wu of Han divided the realm into thirteen provinces, he kept the ancient label Yanzhou for this belt, and later ages let it stand. Yanzhou oversaw eight jurisdictions and fifty-six counties; the census read eighty-three thousand three hundred households.

惠帝之末，兗州闔境淪沒石勒。 後石季龍改陳留郡爲建昌郡，屬洛州。 是時遺黎南渡，元帝僑置兗州，寄居京口。 明帝以郗鑒爲刺史，寄居廣陵，置濮陽、濟陰、高平、太山等郡。 後改爲南兗州，或還江南，或居盱眙，或居山陽。 後始割地爲境，常居廣陵，南與京口對岸。 咸康四年，於北譙界立陳留郡。 安帝分廣陵郡之建陵、臨江、如皋、寧海、蒲濤五縣置山陽郡，屬南兗州。
By the last years of Emperor Hui, not a handbreadth of Yan Province remained free: the whole region had fallen under Shi Le’s heel. Afterward Shi Hu—Jilong by his intimate name—renamed Chenliu as Jianchang and folded it into Luo Province. Survivors poured south across the river; Emperor Yuan therefore “borrowed” a patch of land for a shadow Yan Province, its nominal seat at Jingkou. Emperor Ming named Xi Jian inspector and moved the office to Guangling, carving out nominal jurisdictions—Puyang, Jiyin, Gaoping, Taishan, and more—on paper if not always on soil. Renamed Southern Yan, it drifted: now back below the Yangtze, now perched at Xuyi, now at Shanyang—always provisional, like memory of a lost map. Only later did real territory attach to the name; the inspectorate settled habitually at Guangling, its southern bank staring across the water at Jingkou. In the fourth year of Xiankang they drew a Chenliu Commandery on the frontier of Northern Qiao—another line on the map where refugees might pretend the old heartland still existed. Emperor Ai peeled off Jianling, Linjiang, Rugao, Ninghai, and Putao from Guangling to form a new Shanyang Commandery under Southern Yan—a fresh grid for an old grief.

案禹貢爲荊河之地。 《周禮》：「河南曰豫州。 」豫者舒也，言稟中和之氣，性理安舒也。 《春秋元命包》云：「鉤鈐星別爲豫州。 」地界，西自華山，東至于淮，北自濟，南界荊山。 秦兼天下，以爲三川、河東、南陽、潁川、碭、泗水、薛七郡。 漢改三川爲河南郡，武帝置十三州，豫州舊名不改，以河南、河東二郡屬司隸，又以南陽屬荊州。 先是，改泗水曰沛郡，改碭郡曰梁，改薛曰魯，分梁沛立汝南郡，分潁川立淮陽郡。 後漢章帝改淮陽曰陳郡。 魏武分沛立譙郡，魏文分汝南立弋陽郡。 及武帝受命，又分潁川立襄城郡，分汝南立汝陰郡，合陳郡于梁國。 州統郡國十，縣八十五，戶十一萬六千七百九十六。
The Tribute of Yu draws it as the country between the Jing hills and the great river. The Rites of Zhou declares: ‘South of the river lies Yu Province.’ ‘Yu’ speaks of ease—of a region imbued with balanced breath, whose people grow temperate and unhurried. The apocryphon Spring and Autumn Yuan Ming Bao adds: ‘The hook-and-clasp stars mark out Yu Province among the fields of heaven.’ On earth its borders ran from Mount Hua in the west to the Huai in the east, from the Ji River northward to Mount Jing in the south. When Qin swallowed the world, it sorted this ground into seven commanderies—Sanchuan, Hedong, Nanyang, Yingchuan, Dang, Sishui, and Xue. Han rechristened Sanchuan as Henan; Emperor Wu’s thirteen circuits left the name Yu undisturbed even as Henan and Hedong passed to the capital intendancy and Nanyang was folded into Jing. Already Sishui had become Pei, Dang had become Liang, Xue had turned into Lu; Runan was cut from Liang and Pei, Huaiyang from Yingchuan—the geometry of empire endlessly redrawn. Eastern Han’s Emperor Zhang traded the name Huaiyang for Chen. Cao Cao—posthumously Wei Wu—split Pei to birth Qiao; his son Cao Pi, Wei Wen, split Runan to raise Yiyang. When Sima Yan took the throne, he split Yingchuan again for Xiangcheng, Runan for Ruyin, and wove old Chen into the princedom of Liang. The province held ten commanderies and princedoms, eighty-five counties, and nearly one hundred seventeen thousand households on the books.

案禹貢、《周禮》並爲河內之地，舜置十二牧，則其一也。 《春秋元命包》云：「昴畢散爲冀州，分爲趙國。 」其地有險有易，帝王所都，亂則冀安，弱則冀強，荒則冀豐。 舜以冀州南北闊大，分衛以西爲并州，燕以北爲幽州，周人因焉。 及漢武置十三州，以其地依舊名爲冀州，歷後漢至晉不改。 州統郡國十三，縣八十三，[24]戶三十二萬六千。
By the reckoning of the *Tribute of Yu* and the *Rites of Zhou*, this tract lay within the inner bend of the Yellow River; when Shun divided the realm into twelve pasture-districts, it was counted as one of them. The *Yuanming Bao* gloss on the *Spring and Autumn* records: "When the asterisms Mao and Bi fan outward, they body the substance of Ji Province, which then cleaves into the polity of Zhao." The land itself mingles sheer ridge and gentle plain; emperors and kings have nested their capitals here. In rebellion Ji becomes the sanctuary; in decline Ji becomes the backbone; in drought Ji still runs thick with grain. Because Ji sprawled so far from south to north, Shun carved out everything west of Wei as Bing Province and everything north of Yan as You Province; the Zhou inherited that map and kept it. When Emperor Wu of Han instituted the thirteen provinces, he let this ground keep the ancient name Ji; from Later Han down to Jin no one saw fit to rename it. The province embraced thirteen commanderies and principalities, eighty-three counties, and three hundred twenty-six thousand households.

After Emperor Hui’s reign, Jizhou slid into Shi Le’s grasp. In the second year of Taixing, Shi Le declared himself emperor at Xiangguo and named his state Zhao. Murong Jun later crushed that Zhao; then Fu Jian swept away the Murongs in turn. When Emperor Xiaowu’s eighth Taiyuan year broke Fu Jian’s power, Murong Chui absorbed the ground his armies had held. Murong Chui raised his banner at Zhongshan and history remembers the state as Later Yan. Wei finally rolled up Later Yan’s map.

Youzhou likewise vanished into Shi Le’s orbit once Emperor Hui had passed. In Emperor Mu’s fifth Yonghe year Murong Jun crowned himself at Ji, and chroniclers speak of Former Yan. Two years later Murong Jun carried his court south to Ye. Murong Jun’s death left his heir Murong Wei to face Fu Jian, who erased their throne. When Fu Jian fell, Murong Chui gathered the fragments and styled his realm Later Yan. Murong Chui’s son Murong Bao, seeing the roof collapse, withdrew toward Helong.

案禹貢冀州之域，於周爲幽州界，漢屬右北平郡。 後漢末，公孫度自號平州牧。 及其子康、康子文懿並擅據遼東，東夷九種皆服事焉。 魏置東夷校尉，居襄平，而分遼東、昌黎、玄菟、帶方、樂浪五郡爲平州，後還合爲幽州。 及文懿滅後，有護東夷校尉，居襄平。 咸寧二年十月，分昌黎、遼東、玄菟、帶方、樂浪等郡國五置平州。 統縣二十六，戶一萬八千一百。 [26]
The Tribute of Yu classifies this ground with Jizhou; the Zhou saw it as Youzhou’s marches; Han filed it under Youbeiping. Late in Later Han, Gongsun Du invented the title “shepherd of Pingzhou” and answered to no one. Gongsun Du, then Gongsun Kang, then Gongsun Yuan—who would receive the posthumous title Wenyi—for three generations clamped Liaodong shut, and nine eastern peoples paid them court. Under Wei, a Commandant of the Eastern Yi sat at Xiangping while five frontier commanderies—Liaodong, Changli, Xuantu, Daifang, and Lelang—were carved out as Ping Province, though the whole arrangement was later folded back into You Province. When Gongsun Yuan fell, the court replaced the old post with a Protecting Commandant of the Eastern Yi, again headquartered at Xiangping. In the autumn of the second year of Xianning, the throne peeled away five coastal jurisdictions—Changli, Liaodong, Xuantu, Daifang, and Lelang among them—to form the new province of Ping. Its rolls listed twenty-six counties and eighteen thousand one hundred households. Marginal note twenty-six.

平州初置，以慕容廆爲刺史，遂屬永嘉之亂，廆爲眾所推。 及其孫雋移都于薊。 其後慕容垂子寶又遷于和龍，自幽州至於廬溥鎮以南地入於魏。 慕容熙以幽州刺史鎮令支，青州刺史鎮新城，并州刺史鎮凡城，營州刺史鎮宿軍，冀州刺史鎮肥如。 高雲以幽、冀二州牧鎮肥如，并州刺史鎮白狼。 後爲馮跋所篡，跋僭號於和龍，是爲後燕，卒滅於魏。
Ping Province began its brief life with Murong Hui as inspector, but the Yongjia upheavals soon swept the northeast, and local leaders thrust him to the fore. His grandson Murong Jun later shifted the court north to Ji. Murong Chui's heir Murong Bao dragged the capital onward to Helong, while everything from You Province south through the Lupu garrison belt slid piecemeal into Northern Wei hands. Murong Xi parked his You governor at Lingzhi, his Qing governor at Xincheng, his Bing governor at Fancheng, his Ying governor at Sujun, and his Ji governor at Feiru. Gao Yun coordinated You and Ji from Feiru while his Bing governor held the line at Bailang. Feng Ba eventually seized the throne, proclaimed himself at Helong, and styled his state Later Yan until Wei snuffed it out for good.

Linjin headed the list. The old Dali stronghold, renamed once Qin seized it. A River God temple fronts the Linjin River—cartographers say that is how the county got its name. Next comes Xiagui. Duke Wu of Qin crushed the Gui tribes and marked a new town: because Shanggui already stood upstream, scribes called this one "Lower Gui." Zhongquan and Pinyang followed. Duke Li founded Pinyang on the sunny north shore of the Pin. Suyi, Lianshao, Heyang, and Xiayang filled out the eastern rim. Once called Shaoliang until King Huiwen of Qin rechristened it. Mount Liang looms to the northwest.

Chiyang opens the western cluster. Emperor Hui chartered the county. The jagged spine of Mount Jiezhi rises inside its border. Mei lies farther west. The Chengguo Canal lifts its headgates straight from the Wei. Yong—once the Zhou ritual center—remains a named county. Its chief officer ranked as marquisate prefect. Within Yong's precincts crowd the Five Zhi altars, the cults of Taihao and the Yellow Emperor, and more than three hundred lesser shrines besides. Qian takes its name from the river it straddles. Classic geographers identify Mount Wu to the west with the old name Mount Qian. Chencang and Meiyang border the Qi foothills. Mount Qi guards the northwest—the hill King Tai of Zhou fortified when the Zhou lineage was still young.

惠帝即位，改扶風國爲秦國。 徙都。 [29]建興之後，雍州沒於劉聰。 及劉曜徙都長安，改號曰趙，以秦、涼二州牧鎮上邽，朔州牧鎮高平，幽州刺史鎮北地，并州牧鎮蒲阪。 石勒克長安，復置雍州。 石氏既敗，苻健僭據關中，又都長安，是爲前秦。 於是乃於雍州置司隸校尉，以豫州刺史鎮許昌，秦州刺史鎮上邽，荊州刺史鎮豐陽，洛州刺史鎮宜陽，并州刺史鎮蒲阪。 苻堅時，分司隸爲雍州，分京兆爲咸陽郡，洛州刺史鎮陝城。 滅燕之後，分幽州置平州，鎮龍城，幽州刺史鎮薊城，河州刺史鎮枹罕，并州刺史鎮晉陽，豫州刺史鎮洛陽，兗州刺史鎮倉垣，雍州刺史鎮蒲阪。 於是移洛州居豐陽，以許昌置東豫州，以荊州刺史鎮襄陽，徐州刺史鎮彭城。 既而姚萇滅苻氏，是爲後秦。 及萇子興克洛陽，以并、冀二州牧鎮蒲阪，豫州牧鎮洛陽，兗州刺史鎮倉垣，分司隸領北五郡，置雍州刺史鎮安定。 及姚泓爲劉裕所滅，其地尋入赫連勃勃。 勃勃僭號於統萬，是爲夏。 置幽州牧於大城，又平劉義真於長安，遣子璝鎮焉，號曰南臺。 以朔州牧鎮三城，秦州刺史鎮杏城，雍州刺史鎮陰密，并州刺史鎮蒲阪，梁州牧鎮安定，北秦州刺史鎮武功，豫州牧鎮李閏，[30]荊州刺史鎮陝，其州郡之名並不可知也。 然自元帝渡江，所置州亦皆遙領。 初以魏該爲雍州刺史，鎮酇城，尋省，僑立始平郡，寄居武當城。 有秦國流人至江南，改堂邑爲秦郡，僑立尉氏縣屬焉。 康帝時，庾翼爲荊州刺史，遷鎮襄陽。 其後秦雍流人多南出樊沔，孝武始於襄陽僑立雍州，仍立京兆、始平、扶風、河南、廣平、義成、北河南七郡，並屬襄陽。 襄陽故屬荊州。
On Emperor Hui’s accession the court redesignated the Fufeng fief as the state of Qin. They shifted the seat of government. Once the Jianxing era ended, Yongzhou slipped from Jin hands into Liu Cong’s Zhao realm. After Liu Yao relocated his court to Chang’an and proclaimed the Zhao regime, he posted the joint stewards of Qin and Liang at Shanggui, the Shuozhou steward at Gaoping, the Youzhou governor at Beidi, and the Bingzhou steward at Puban. Shi Le’s victory at Chang’an brought Yongzhou back onto the map. The Shi house collapsed; Fu Jian then claimed Guanzhong, moved his capital once more to Chang’an, and so began Former Qin. Within Yongzhou he installed a metropolitan intendant; he anchored Yuzhou at Xuchang, Qinzhou at Shanggui, Jingzhou at Fengyang, Luozhou at Yiyang, and Bingzhou at Puban. Fu Jian cleaved the metropolitan circuit into a separate Yongzhou, carved Xianyang commandery out of Jingzhao, and redeployed the Luozhou governor to the Shancheng salient. His conquest of Yan prompted a new Pingzhou carved from Youzhou with Longcheng as its hinge; Youzhou itself held Ji, Hezhou watched Fuhan, Bingzhou guarded Jinyang, Yuzhou sat on Luoyang, Yanzhou locked Cangyuan, and Yongzhou returned to Puban. Luozhou slid south to Fengyang, Xuchang hosted a shadow Eastern Yuzhou, Jingzhou’s governor pulled back to Xiangyang, and Xuzhou’s to Pengcheng. Soon Yao Chang swept away the Fu house and styled his realm Later Qin. Yao Xing’s capture of Luoyang fixed the joint Bing-Ji command at Puban, Yuzhou’s steward at Luoyang, Yanzhou at Cangyuan, while a truncated Sili oversaw five northern counties and a Yongzhou governor held Anding. Liu Yu’s annihilation of Yao Hong left the plateau open; Helian Bobo wasted little time absorbing it. At Tongwan, Helian Bobo declared himself emperor of the Xia dynasty that history remembers as Helian Xia. He stationed a Youzhou steward at Dacheng, crushed Liu Yizhen’s remnant in Chang’an, and left his son Gui there as viceregent under the epithet Southern Terrace. Shuozhou anchored Sancheng, Qinzhou Xingcheng, Yongzhou Yinmi, Bingzhou Puban, Liangzhou Anding, northern Qinzhou Wugong, Yuzhou the Li Run basin, Jingzhou the Shan ford—yet scribal memory of those ephemeral divisions barely survived. Still, once Emperor Yuan ferried the court south, every new province Jin proclaimed existed only as a title held from afar. The court first named Wei Gai Yongzhou governor with headquarters at Zancheng, withdrew the post almost at once, then floated a paper Shiping commandery housed inside Wudang’s walls. Qin exiles who washed up along the lower Yangtze persuaded officials to rechristen Tangyi as Qin commandery and hang a nominal Weishi county beneath it. Under Emperor Kang, Yu Yi’s Jingzhou portfolio moved its forward base upriver to Xiangyang. Later waves fleeing Qin and Yong spilled through Fan and Mian; Emperor Xiaowu answered by planting a shadow Yongzhou in Xiangyang alongside seven satellite commanderies—Jingzhao, Shiping, Fufeng, Henan, Guangping, Yicheng, and northern Henan—all reporting to the same southern hub. Xiangyang had long been a Jingzhou town before this layered administration.
154
案禹貢雍州之西界，周衰，其地爲狄。 秦興美陽甘泉宮，本匈奴鑄金人祭天之處。 匈奴既失甘泉，又使休屠、渾邪王等居涼州之地。 二王後以地降漢，漢置張掖、酒泉、敦煌、武威郡。 其後又置金城郡，謂之河西五郡。 漢改周之雍州爲涼州，蓋以地處西方，常寒涼也。 地勢西北邪出，在南山之間，南隔西羌，西通西域，于時號爲斷匈奴右臂。 獻帝時，涼州數有亂，河西五郡去州隔遠，於是乃別以爲雍州。 末又依古典定九州，乃合關右以爲雍州。 魏時復分以爲涼州，刺史領戊己校尉，護西域，如漢故事，至晉不改。 統郡八，縣四十六，戶三萬七百。
The Yugong atlas draws Yongzhou’s western edge across ground that, once Zhou authority frayed, fell to Di pastoralists. Qin builders raised Ganquan Palace near Meiyang atop a Xiongnu altar where great bronze effigies once received skyward offerings. Deprived of Ganquan, the confederation resettled the Xiutu and Hunye kings and their followings across what would become Liangzhou pasture. Those two kings eventually yielded their ranges to Han, which organized the corridor into Zhangye, Jiuquan, Dunhuang, and Wuwei. Jincheng was added later, completing the famous pentad of Hexi commanderies. Han mapmakers retired Zhou’s Yongzhou label for the west in favor of Liangzhou—cold frontier, high sky, wind that never quite warms. The corridor runs northwest between southern ranges, screens the Qiang on one flank and opens toward the Tarim on the other; strategists called it cleaving the Xiongnu’s sword arm. Emperor Xian’s reign saw Liangzhou convulsed so often that the five Hexi prefectures, sundered from the provincial seat, were hived off as a separate Yongzhou. Late Han surveyors, nostalgic for the ninefold Yugong grid, folded the entire Guanyou plateau back into a single Yongzhou. Wei restored a stand-alone Liangzhou whose governors, like their Han forebears, doubled as wuji colonels shepherding the Western Regions—a practice Jin left untouched. The province embraced eight commanderies, forty-six counties, and thirty thousand seven hundred households.

元康五年，惠帝分敦煌郡之宜禾、伊吾、冥安、深泉、廣至等五縣，分酒泉之沙頭縣，又別立會稽、新鄉，凡八縣爲晉昌郡。 永寧中，張軌爲涼州刺史，鎮武威，上表請合秦雍流移人於姑臧西北，置武興郡，統武興、大城、烏支、襄武、晏然、新鄣、平狄、司監等縣。 又分西平界置晉興郡，統晉興、枹罕、永固、臨津、臨鄣、廣昌、大夏、遂興、罕唐、左南等縣。 是時中原淪沒，元帝徙居江左，軌乃控據河西，稱晉正朔，是爲前涼。 及張寔，分金城之令居、枝陽二縣，又立永登縣，合三縣立廣武郡。 張茂分武興、金城、西平、安故爲定州。 張駿分武威、武興、西平、張掖、酒泉、建康、西海、西郡、湟河、晉興、廣武合十一郡爲涼州，[34]興晉、金城、武始、南安、永晉、大夏、武成、漢中爲河州，敦煌、晉昌、高昌、西域都護、戊己校尉、玉門大護軍三郡三營爲沙州。 [35]張駿假涼州都督，攝三州。 張祚又以敦煌郡爲商州。 永興中，置漢陽縣以守牧地，張玄靚改爲祁連郡。 張天錫又別置臨松郡。 天錫降於苻氏，其地尋爲呂光所據。 呂光都於姑臧後，以郭黁言讖，改昌松爲東張掖郡。 及呂隆降於姚興，其地三分。 武昭王爲西涼，建號於敦煌。 禿髮烏孤爲南涼，建號於樂都。 沮渠蒙遜爲北涼，建號於張掖。 而分據河西五郡。
Yuankang’s fifth year saw Emperor Hui peel Yihe, Yiwu, Ming’an, Shenquan, and Guangzhi from Dunhuang, lift Shatou from Jiuquan, and mint fresh Kuaiji and Xinxiang registers—eight counties in all under a new Jinchang commandery. Midway through Yongning, Liangzhou governor Zhang Gui, encamped at Wuwei, asked the throne to gather Qin-Yong exiles beyond northwest Guzang into a Wuxing commandery built around seats named Wuxing, Dacheng, Wuzhi, Xiangwu, Yanran, Xinzhang, Pingdi, and Sijian. He likewise trimmed Xiping to raise Jinxing commandery—seats at Jinxing, Fuhan, Yonggu, Linjin, Linzhang, Guangchang, Daxia, Suixing, Hantang, Zuonan, and more. While the Central Plains drowned in war and Emperor Yuan beached his court south of the great river, Zhang Gui clasped the Hexi corridor, flew Jin’s banner, and so founded what historians call Former Liang. Under Zhang Shi, Lingju and Zhiyang—two counties carved from Jincheng—were joined with newly founded Yongdeng, and the trio became Guangwu Commandery. Zhang Mao formed Ding Province from Wuxing, Jincheng, Xiping, and Angu. Zhang Jun organized Liang Province out of eleven commanderies: Wuwei, Wuxing, Xiping, Zhangye, Jiuquan, Jiankang, Xihai, Xijun, Huanghe, Jinxing, and Guangwu. He drew He Province from Xingjin, Jincheng, Wushi, Nan'an, Yongjin, Daxia, Wucheng, and Hanzhong. Sha Province bundled Dunhuang, Jinchang, and Gaochang with the Western Regions protectorate, the Wuji colonelcy, and the Yumen grand protectorate—three civil jurisdictions and three encampments. Zhang Jun served as acting governor-general of Liang and held all three provinces in his portfolio. Zhang Zuo turned Dunhuang Commandery into Shang Province. Mid-Yongxing saw Hanyang County founded to watch the grazing country; Zhang Xuanjing later elevated the district to Qilian Commandery. Zhang Tianxi added an independent Linsong Commandery. After Tianxi yielded to the Fu house, Lü Guang seized the ground almost at once. Once Lü Guang ruled from Guzang, a prophecy uttered by Guo Nen moved him to rename Changsong Eastern Zhangye. Lü Long’s submission to Yao Xing left the realm split among three claimants. The Prince of Wuzhao founded Western Liang, raising his banner at Dunhuang. Tufa Wugu proclaimed Southern Liang with his seat at Ledu. Juqu Mengxun forged Northern Liang, enthroned in spirit at Zhangye. Between them they partitioned the five Hexi commanderies.

The classic text places this land in old Yong. Wei first peeled Longyou away as a province whose governor doubled as Colonel Protecting the Qiang, though the office flickered out for a time midstream. In Taishi 5, Yong’s five Longyou commanderies, Jincheng from the northwestern Liang, and Yinping from the southern Liang—seven units altogether—were folded into a revived Qin Province headquartered at Jicheng. Taikang 3 abolished Qin Province and swallowed it back into Yong. The seventh year saw it rise again, now anchored at Shanggui. Its register held six commanderies, twenty-four counties, and thirty-two thousand one hundred households.

案禹貢華陽黑水之地，舜置十二牧，則其一也。 梁者，言西方金剛之氣強梁，故因名焉。 《周禮》職方氏以梁并雍。 漢不立州名，以其地爲益州。 及獻帝初平六年，[38]以臨江縣屬永寧郡。 建安六年，劉璋改永寧爲巴東郡，分巴郡墊江置巴西郡。 劉備據蜀，又分廣漢之葭萌、涪城、梓潼、白水四縣，改葭萌曰漢壽，又立漢德縣，以爲梓潼郡； 割巴郡之宕渠、宣漢、漢昌三縣置宕渠郡，尋省，以縣並屬巴西郡。 泰始三年，分益州，立梁州於漢中，改漢壽爲晉壽，又分廣漢置新都郡。 梁州統郡八，縣四十四，[39]戶七萬六千三百。
The Tribute of Yu draws this terrain between Huayang and the Blackwater, one of the twelve pastures Shun entrusted to his herdsmen. The name Liang speaks of the western edge’s stern, metallic vigor—unyielding force—crystallized in a single word. The Zhou ritual canon had the cartographer fold Liang into Yong. Han never titled the region a zhou of its own; everything here counted as Yizhou. In the sixth year of Emperor Xian’s Chuping reign, Linjiang County was folded under Yongning. Jian'an 6 saw Liu Zhang rename Yongning as Badong and spin Dianjiang out of Ba to seed Baxi. When Liu Bei seized Shu he carved four Guanghan counties—Jiameng, Fucheng, Zitong, and Baishui—renamed Jiameng Hanshou, added Hande, and drew the lot into Zitong Commandery; he tried to hive Dangqu, Xuanhan, and Hangchang off Ba as Dangqu Commandery, though the experiment was short-lived and those towns soon returned to Baxi. Taishi 3 split Yizhou to seat Liang Province in Hanzhong, retitled Hanshou as Jinshou, and broke another slice from Guanghan for Xindu. Liang’s rolls listed eight commanderies, forty-four counties, and seventy-six thousand three hundred households.

太康六年九月，罷新都郡并廣漢郡。 惠帝復分巴西置宕渠郡，統宕渠、漢昌、宣漢三縣，并以新城、魏興、上庸合四郡以屬梁州。 尋而梁州郡縣沒于李特，永嘉中又分屬楊茂搜，其晉人流寓於梁益者，仍於二州立南北二陰平郡。 及桓溫平蜀之後，以巴漢流人立晉昌郡，領長樂、安晉、延壽、安樂、宣漢、寧都、新興、吉陽、東關、永安十縣； 又置益昌、晉興二縣，屬巴西郡； 於德陽界東南置遂寧郡； 又於晉壽置劍閣縣，屬梁州。 後孝武分梓潼北界立晉壽郡，統晉壽、白水、邵歡、興安四縣； 梓潼郡徙居梓潼，罷劍閣縣； 又別置南漢中郡，分巴西、梓潼爲金山郡。 及安帝時，又立新巴、汶陽二郡，又有北新巴、華陽、南陰平、北陰平四郡，其後又立巴渠、懷安、宋熙、白水、上洛、北上洛、南宕渠、懷漢、新興、安康等十郡。
Ninth month, Taikang 6: Xindu Commandery vanished into Guanghan. Emperor Hui peeled Baxi again to resurrect Dangqu over three counties, then yoked that package with Xincheng, Weixing, and Shangyong—four commanderies—to Liang. Liang’s map soon washed into Li Te’s hands; Yongjia saw pieces fall to Yang Maosou; Jin exiles caught between Liang and Yi kept stringing up paired Yinping commanderies, north and south. Once Huan Wen stilled Shu, he settled Ba-Han refugees in a new Jinchang Commandery spanning ten counties: Changle, Anjin, Yanshou, Anle, Xuanhan, Ningdu, Xinxing, Jiyang, Dongguan, and Yong'an; he tucked Yichang and Jinxing under Baxi as well; and along Deyang’s southeast marches he opened Suining Commandery. They also founded Jiange County at Jinshou and placed it under Liang Province. Later Emperor Xiaowu carved the northern rim of Zitong into Jinshou Commandery, which ruled the four counties of Jinshou, Baishui, Shaohuan, and Xing'an. The seat of Zitong Commandery was shifted to Zitong proper, and Jiange County was abolished. A separate Nanhanzhong Commandery was also established, and lands taken from Baxi and Zitong were gathered into Jinshan Commandery. Under Emperor An the court added Xinba and Wenyang, followed by four more—Northern Xinba, Huayang, Southern Yinping, and Northern Yinping—and later founded another ten, among them Baqu, Huai'an, Songxi, Baishui, Shangluo, Northern Shangluo, Southern Dangqu, Huaihan, Xinxing, and Ankang.
204
案禹貢及舜十二牧俱爲梁州之域，周合梁於雍，則又爲雍州之地。 《春秋元命包》云：「參伐流爲益州，益之爲言阨也。 」言其所在之地險阨也，亦曰疆壤益大，故以名焉。 始秦惠王滅蜀，置郡，以張若爲蜀守。 及始皇置三十六郡，蜀郡之名不改。 漢初有漢中、巴、蜀。 高祖六年，分蜀置廣漢，凡爲四郡。 武帝開西南夷，更置犍爲、牂柯、越巂、益州四郡，凡八郡，遂置益州統焉，益州蓋始此也。 及後漢，明帝以新附置永昌郡，安帝又以諸道置蜀、廣漢、犍爲三郡屬國都尉，及靈帝又以汶江、蠶陵、廣柔三縣立汶山郡。 獻帝初平元年，劉璋分巴郡立永寧郡。 [42]建安六年，改永寧爲巴東，以巴郡爲巴西，又立涪陵郡。 二十一年，劉備分巴郡立固陵郡。 蜀章武元年又改固陵爲巴東郡，巴西郡爲巴郡，又分廣漢立梓潼郡，分犍爲立江陽郡，以蜀郡屬國爲漢嘉郡，以犍爲屬國爲朱提郡。 劉禪建興二年，改益州郡爲建寧郡，廣漢屬國爲陰平郡，分建寧永昌立雲南郡，分建寧牂柯立興古郡，分廣漢立東廣漢郡。 魏景元中，蜀平，省東廣漢郡。 及武帝泰始二年，分益州置梁州，以漢中屬焉。 七年，又分益州置寧州。 益州統郡八，縣四十四，戶十四萬九千三百。
The "Tribute of Yu" and the twelve shepherds of Shun alike mapped this country inside Liang Province; when the Zhou folded Liang into Yong, the same hills and rivers became territory of Yong Province. The *Chunqiu Yuanming Bao* says: "The constellation of Shen and Fa spilled their light downward to become Yizhou; the syllable *yi* is a word for straitened defiles." "—in other words, its ground is perilous and tight hemmed—and some also say its frontiers ever widened, which is why the name took hold." When King Hui of Qin extinguished Shu, he laid out a commandery and named Zhang Ruo its governor. Once the First Emperor fixed the realm at thirty-six commanderies, the old name Shu Commandery still stood. In the founding years of Han the southwest still answered to Hanzhong, Ba, and Shu. In the sixth year of Gaozu's reign, Shu was split to create Guanghan, making four commanderies in all. Emperor Wu opened the southwestern tribes and added Qianwei, Zangke, Yuexi, and Yizhou—eight commanderies altogether—then set a Yizhou superintendency above them; the great province of Yizhou, one may say, begins here. Under the Later Han, Mingdi carved Yongchang from fresh conquests; Andi appointed commandants for dependent states attached to Shu, Guanghan, and Qianwei; and Lingdi raised Wenshan Commandery from the three counties of Wenjiang, Canling, and Guangrou. In the first Chuping year of Emperor Xian, Liu Zhang broke Yongning Commandery out of Ba. In the sixth year of Jian'an, Yongning became Badong, the old Ba Commandery was renamed Baxi, and Fuling Commandery was founded besides. In the twenty-first year of the same reign arc, Liu Bei set Guling Commandery apart from Ba. In the first Zhangwu year of Shu, Guling was rechristened Badong, Baxi reverted to Ba, Zitong rose from a partition of Guanghan, Jiangyang from Qianwei, the Shu dependent state became Hanjia Commandery, and the Qianwei dependent state became Zhuti Commandery. In Liu Shan's second Jianxing year, Yizhou Commandery was renamed Jianning, the Guanghan dependent state became Yinping, Yunnan was formed from Jianning and Yongchang, Xingu from Jianning and Zangke, and Eastern Guanghan from a further cut of Guanghan. Midway through Wei's Jingyuan era, after Shu had been subdued, Eastern Guanghan Commandery was abolished. In the second Tai shi year of Emperor Wu, Liang Province was severed from Yizhou, and Hanzhong was transferred to the new division. Seven years later, another share of Yizhou was reassembled into Ning Province. Yizhou oversaw eight commanderies and forty-four counties, registering one hundred forty-nine thousand three hundred households.

惠帝之後，李特僭號於蜀，稱漢，益州郡縣皆沒于特。 李雄又分漢嘉、蜀二郡立沈黎、漢原二郡。 是時益州郡縣雖沒李氏，江左並遙置之。 桓溫滅蜀，其地復爲晉有，省漢原、沈黎而立南陰平、晉原、寧蜀、始寧四郡焉。 咸安二年，益州復沒於苻氏。 太元八年，復爲晉有。 隆安二年，又立晉熙、遂寧、晉寧三郡云。
After Emperor Hui's day, Li Te seized a kingly style in Shu, styled his polity Han, and every commandery and county of Yizhou slid beneath his banner. Li Xiong next split Hanjia and Shu to raise the paired commanderies of Shenli and Hanyuan. Even while Li's line held the Yizhou registers, the court east of the Yangtze kept naming officials to those posts from afar. When Huan Wen crushed Shu, the soil returned to Jin, which struck Hanyuan and Shenli from the map and planted four fresh commanderies—Southern Yinping, Jinyuan, Ningshu, and Shining—in their place. In the second Xian'an year Yizhou sank once more under the Fu dynasty of Former Qin. By the eighth year of Taiyuan it belonged to Jin again. The second Long'an year reportedly saw the founding of Jinxi, Suining, and Jinning commanderies.

Across Han and Wei this had been heartland of Yizhou. In the seventh Taishi year, Emperor Wu judged Yizhou too sprawling and folded Jianning, Xingu, and Yunnan from it together with Yongchang out of Jiaozhou—four commanderies—to constitute Ning Province, with forty-five counties and eighty-three thousand households on its books.

太康三年，武帝又廢寧州入益州，立南夷校尉以護之。 太安二年，惠帝復置寧州，又分建寧以西七縣別立爲益州郡。 永嘉二年，改益州郡曰晉寧，分牂柯立平夷、夜郎二郡。 [47]然是時其地再爲李特所有。 其後李壽分寧州興古、永昌、雲南、朱提、越巂、河陽六郡爲漢州。 咸康四年，分牂柯、夜郎、朱提、越巂四郡置安州。 八年，又罷并寧州，以越巂還屬益州，省永昌郡焉。
In Taikang three, Emperor Wu abolished Ning Province and folded it back into Yizhou, creating a Colonel of the Southern Tribes to watch over the frontier. Tai'an two saw Emperor Hui revive Ning Province and peel seven counties west of Jianning into a stand-alone Yizhou Commandery. In the second Yongjia year Yizhou Commandery was rebaptized Jinning, while Pingyi and Yelang were broken out of Zangke. Yet the ground had once more slipped into Li Te's grasp. Later Li Shou drafted six commanderies—Xingu, Yongchang, Yunnan, Zhuti, Yuexi, and Heyang—from Ning Province to constitute Han Province. The fourth Xiankang year established An Province from the four commanderies of Zangke, Yelang, Zhuti, and Yuexi. Eight years on, An was rescinded and merged back into Ning Province, Yuexi was returned to Yizhou's orbit, and Yongchang Commandery vanished from the rolls.

The treatise first said “Jiyang commandery” where it should name Jiyin. Commentarial note: the Han never had a Jiyang commandery; “Jiyang” is almost certainly a scribal slip for Jiyin. Bi Gun’s biography calls him a native of Yuanqu in Jiyin, and the Song shu’s gazetteer notes for both Chengwu and Lihu cite the Jin Taikang geography to show they lay within Jiyin. Du Yu’s gloss on the seventh year of Duke Yin in the Zuo zhuan, together with Xi Shen’s biography, corroborate the point. The text is emended on that evidence.
